title: A Pimple or Bump on the Gum Near a Tooth: What It Means
metaTitle: Bump on the Gum Near a Tooth: What It Means
metaDescription: A pimple or bump on the gum near a tooth is often a draining infection called a sinus tract. Learn why it comes and goes and why it needs treatment in Markham.
excerpt: A pimple-like bump on the gum is often a sinus tract - a sign that infection from a tooth is draining. It can come and go, but it still needs treatment to heal.
heroImageAlt: Close-up of a gum with a small white bump above a tooth, indicating a possible sinus tract.
bodyHtml:
That small pimple or bump on the gum near a tooth is most often a sign of a chronic infection that has found a way to drain. Known as a sinus tract or gum boil, it forms when pus from an infected tooth or the surrounding bone pushes a channel through the gum to the surface. It can look like a little white, yellow, or red blister, it may leak a salty or unpleasant-tasting fluid, and it often comes and goes. The important point is this: even when it is painless or seems to heal, the bump usually means an underlying problem still needs treatment.

Why a gum bump appears

When the pulp inside a tooth becomes infected, bacteria and pus build up around the tip of the root. Your body looks for a release valve, and sometimes that pressure tunnels through the bone and gum, creating a sinus tract. The visible bump is simply the opening of that channel. Because it relieves pressure, people often notice that their toothache improved around the time the bump showed up. That relief is misleading. The infection has not resolved; it has only found somewhere to drain.

Less commonly, a bump near a tooth can come from gum disease, a piece of trapped food or debris under the gum, or irritation. A dentist can tell these apart, often with an X-ray that reveals infection at the root tip and sometimes by tracing the tract with a thin material to find its source.

Why it tends to come and go

A sinus tract can open, drain, and appear to close, then return days or weeks later. This cycle happens because the source of the infection remains active even while the drainage point heals over temporarily. Many people wait, hoping it will disappear for good. In reality, a repeatedly returning gum bump is the body signalling an ongoing infection that will keep recurring until the cause is treated.

Why treatment matters even without pain

It is tempting to ignore something that does not hurt, but a draining infection can quietly damage the bone around the tooth over time. Addressing the source, often through root canal treatment to remove the infected pulp, or occasionally extraction if the tooth cannot be saved, allows the tract to heal and protects the surrounding tissue. Antibiotics alone do not fix the problem because they do not remove the infected tissue at the centre of it.

Should I try to pop the bump?

No. Squeezing or popping a gum boil will not treat the infection and can irritate the area. Gentle warm salt-water rinses can keep it clean while you arrange a dental visit, but the bump needs professional assessment to find and treat its cause.

Is a gum bump an emergency?

A small, slowly draining bump is usually not an emergency, but it should be examined soon. If you develop spreading facial swelling, fever, or significant pain, treat that as urgent and seek care promptly, because it can mean the infection is becoming more active.

How is the cause found?

Your dentist will examine the area, check which tooth responds to testing, and typically take an X-ray. Because the bump can sit a little distance from the actual problem tooth, imaging helps confirm the real source before treatment begins.

Having a gum bump checked in Markham

If you keep noticing a pimple-like bump on your gum, even one that fades and returns, it is worth having it assessed rather than waiting it out. You can learn more about the practice through the team at Smile Dental Arts Centre, and their endodontics information explains how infections inside a tooth are commonly treated. Patients across the GTA, including those in North York considering care in Markham, are welcome to reach out. A recurring gum bump is a solvable problem, and getting to its cause is what allows it to heal for good.
